title: Many ways of being Muslim
hook: one faith lived in many languages, customs and schools

segments.voice: Yesterday closed the festival year with days for everyone: the poor fed before the prayer, the orphan and the traveler at the table. Your line was no one alone on eid. Did the invitation go out? Today, a new stretch: Islam in the world today. Day one thousand three hundred sixty-seven.

One row at Friday prayer in a big city mosque, shoulder to shoulder. A taxi driver who grew up speaking Somali. A student from Indonesia. A grandfather from Lahore in a crisp white shalwar kameez. A convert who learned the prayer not long ago and still watches the person beside him for the next move. After the prayer they'll go home to different kitchens and different languages. But right now the imam says Allahu akbar, the same words of al-Fatiha are recited in Arabic, and the whole row stands facing the same direction. Today, one faith, lived many ways.
screen: `ONE ROW, MANY HOMES.` → `THE SAME FATIHA.` → `THE SAME DIRECTION.`

segments.voice: Start with a verse the Qur'an addresses to everyone. Surah al-Hujurat, in Pickthall's translation: "O mankind! Lo! We have created you male and female, and have made you nations and tribes that ye may know one another." Nations and tribes aren't treated as a problem to be solved. They're there so people can get to know each other. And the verse goes straight on: "Lo! the noblest of you, in the sight of Allah, is the best in conduct." Second, the Qur'an counts difference among Allah's signs. Surah al-Rum lists the creation of the heavens and the earth, and then, in the same breath, "the difference of your languages and colours." A world of accents, on purpose. Third, schools. Muslims who pray the same prayer sometimes pray it a little differently. Among Sunni Muslims there are the schools of law named for their teachers: Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi'i, Hanbali. Among Shia Muslims, the Ja'fari school, and there are Ibadi Muslims as well. In some mosques you'll see people standing with their hands folded, and in others with their arms at their sides. Each is following a school with its own scholars and its own reasons. Fourth, customs. What's cooked for Eid, what's worn to Friday prayer, how a wedding goes: these grow from places, not only from texts. And through all of it, the center holds: the shahadah, the prayer in Arabic, the same qibla. Sahih Muslim reports the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, saying, in paraphrase, that Allah doesn't look at your outward forms or your wealth, but at your hearts and your deeds.
screen: `NATIONS AND TRIBES, TO KNOW EACH OTHER.` · `LANGUAGES AMONG HIS SIGNS.` · `SCHOOLS: ONE PRAYER, SEVERAL WAYS.` · `CUSTOMS GROW FROM PLACES.`

segments.voice: The practice: learn about a Muslim culture new to you. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind the Muslims you've seen or known, and notice where they come from. Then think of a place you've never connected with Islam at all. Senegal. Bosnia. China. Trinidad. The Philippines. Just pick one that's new to you. Sit with the question for a minute: what would Friday look like there? What would Eid smell like? You don't need the answers yet. Just let the picture be blank and curious. If you pray, you can remember the people of that place. The bell holds the time.
Many ways of being Muslim. One faith, kept in many languages, customs and schools of law, with the same prayer at its center. Today's word.
screen: `MANY WAYS OF BEING MUSLIM — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: one faith, many ways. Today, look up one thing about how Muslims keep Friday or Eid in the place you picked. Tomorrow, the mosque community. Day one thousand three hundred sixty-seven.

howItsDone: Muslims in many countries share the shahadah, the daily prayers in Arabic and the qibla toward Makkah, while following different schools of law and keeping the customs, languages and foods of their own places.

original.note: Arabic: "nations and tribes," from Surah al-Hujurat 49:13.

trapdoor: what you thought: Muslims are all the same.
what it means: one faith, one prayer, one qibla, kept in many languages, schools of law and local customs.
what a scholar hears: al-Hujurat 49:13 on nations and tribes, al-Rum 30:22 on languages as signs, and the schools that pray one prayer in several ways.

Confirm the details (Somali, Indonesia, Lahore, a convert) are fair and not stereotyping.
Arms at the sides in prayer (sadl) is associated with many Malikis and with Shia practice; the script does not name which school does which. Confirm.
The schools are named, not counted, under the claims rule. Ibadi Muslims are mentioned briefly; confirm wording.
